records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new OR branch in deleteMany deletes any SMS WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 regardless of scheduledDate, so the scheduledDate condition no longer bounds deletion. A reminder that failed twice (retryCount=2) but whose scheduled date is still days in the future is permanently deleted on the next cron run, so that recipient never receives any SMS — the retry cap silently becomes a hard drop even when there was ample time to retry later. Anyone running overlapping deployments or frequent cron invocations gets bitten.
records.rationale: The diff changes `deleteMany` to `where: { OR: [ { method: SMS, scheduledDate: { lte: now } }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } } ] }`, so any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1` will be deleted regardless of `scheduledDate` (and even regardless of `method`, since the second OR branch has no method filter). This matches the finding that the scheduledDate bound no longer applies for retryCount-based deletion, causing reminders to be permanently dropped after 2 failures even if still scheduled in the future, contradicting the comment intent.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The prisma.workflowReminder.update inside the catch block is itself unguarded, so if it throws (e.g., P2025 because the row was concurrently deleted by another run's deleteMany) the rejection escapes the catch that was supposed to make the loop resilient. A single failed bookkeeping update aborts the whole for-loop, skipping every remaining reminder in that run; the operator sees only a generic error and reminders silently stop being scheduled for that cycle.
records.rationale: In the per-reminder try/catch, the catch block now does `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ where: { id: reminder.id }, data: { retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 } })` with no guarding. If that update throws (e.g., record not found), it will escape the catch and reject the handler, aborting the loop and skipping remaining reminders. This is plausible given the diff also adds a `deleteMany` with `OR: [...] { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`, making concurrent/earlier deletion of the same reminder ID possible before the catch update runs.

A transient Twilio failure twice in a row causes the reminder to be permanently deleted instead of retried or marked failed — the user never gets the SMS and the record is gone, losing audit state; the original query only deleted past-dated reminders.

Once a reminder of any method hits retryCount 2, the next cron run hard-deletes it, so email/other-channel reminders stop being sent and bookings lose those reminders entirely — no cancellation event, no audit; the stated intent (SMS retry count tracking) does not authorize deleting non-SMS rows.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The else branch increments retryCount on the non-scheduling path (when a scheduled SMS was found), so a reminder that is already successfully scheduled gets its retry counter incremented each cron run and is then deleted by the deleteMany retryCount > 1 clause. An already-scheduled SMS reminder is re-fetched every run (the findMany has no retryCount/scheduled filter shown), its retryCount climbs by 1 per run, and after 3 cron runs the deleteMany branch removes it from the DB — successfully scheduled reminders self-destruct, breaking the retry invariant the PR claims to enforce.
records.rationale: The finding misreads the control flow. In the diff, `retryCount` is incremented only in the `else` branch when **no** scheduled SMS is found, not when one is found: `if (scheduledSMS) { ... } else { ... retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 }` (and also in `catch`). When `scheduledSMS` exists, the code updates `referenceId` and does not increment `retryCount`, so “already successfully scheduled reminders get their retry counter incremented each cron run” is contradicted by the shown logic.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The new OR branch in deleteMany drops the method and scheduledDate filters, deleting any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 regardless of method or scheduled date. A reminder that failed scheduling twice is silently and permanently deleted on the next run — it never sends and leaves no record; the deletion also applies to future-scheduled rows and would delete non-SMS reminders if any other path ever increments retryCount. Users simply stop receiving reminders with no failure state, since the delete fires unconditionally at the top of every invocation.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] retryCount is incremented from the stale in-memory value (reminder.retryCount + 1) rather than an atomic increment, in a cron handler that can run concurrently with itself. Two overlapping invocations of this endpoint read the same retryCount and each write the same +1, undercounting actual retry attempts and delaying the cap by one extra round of API calls to Twilio per reminder per race.
records.rationale: The diff shows `retryCount` being updated using a read-modify-write based on the in-memory `reminder.retryCount` value: `data: { retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 }` (added in both the `else` branch and the `catch`). If two invocations process the same reminder concurrently after both reading the same `retryCount`, they can both write the same incremented value, losing one increment. An atomic increment (`{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`) would avoid this race.

Operators relying on this cron to actually retry failed SMS reminders see reminders vanish after a single retry, and reminders deleted via the retryCount>1 predicate are removed even while still scheduled in Twilio, leaving orphaned scheduled SMS that will fire with no corresponding WorkflowReminder row. No test in this diff exercises the deleteMany OR predicate, the retryCount increment on the error path, or the else-branch increment, so none of this is verified.

Reminders that are legitimately absent from the Twilio response get their retryCount incremented toward the deleteMany threshold, and a race between the findMany and the listSMS call can cause a valid reminder to be deleted after two cron runs. No test distinguishes the else-branch from the catch-branch, and neither new increment path nor the new deleteMany predicate has any test coverage in this diff (no test-shaped files changed at all — verified by scanning the diff).
